utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. Case Number IT-95-10-PT, the Prosecutor against Ranko Cesic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Cesic, I'd first like to know whether you can hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was on the wrong channel, but I read that your answer was that you can hear me. Yes, please be seated, Mr. Cesic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I first have the appearances of the parties. Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. My name is Mark Harmon. To my right, Mr. Vladimir Tochilovsky; to his right, Mr. Tom Hannis, and to his right, the case manager, Susan Grogan. And we represent the Office of the Prosecutor in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. My name is Mihajlo Bakrac. I am representing the accused Ranko Cesic in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. I first have to draw the attention of the public, because the parties are already aware of it, of two orders that have been filed yesterday confidentially. The orders -- one of the orders reschedules this meeting which was expected to be a 65 ter meeting into a meeting where we will hear a -- I'll just give the names of the orders. The one is called "order to convert a Status Conference into a hearing to entertain a joint motion for consideration of the plea agreement between the Prosecutor and Ranko Cesic." The other order is an order designating a Chamber in which the constitution of this Chamber is further explained, specifically that I am presiding in this case. The confidentiality of these orders is lifted on from this moment. So we are here now, as the order says, to hear a joint motion, and I do understand, but let me just seek confirmation of it, that the filing of documents pursuant to Rule 65 ter is understood by the parties as a request to hear a joint motion on the attached plea agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, that is correct. May I just say that in respect of questions the Chamber may have about this agreement, I'm prepared to have Mr. Tochilovsky address the Chamber in all respects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon. Is this also the understanding of you, that the filing of documents is to be understood as a request to hear the joint motion on a plea agreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I am in full agreement with my learned colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Bakrac. So we'll then perhaps ask some questions on the plea agreement that has been filed. As the Rules say, a plea agreement should be made public unless there are reasons not to do so. Do I understand the position of the parties to be, because that's what I read in the filing of documents pursuant to Rule 62 ter, that the parties want the plea agreement to be released as public, as a public document? So that means in full publicity?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. That's also the view of the Defence, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore we can deal with the plea agreement in full detail in an open session. First of all, the Chamber establishes that there is a plea agreement, and I'd like to know, Mr. Cesic, whether the signatures I find on the copy that has been provided to you is your signature. Could, perhaps, the usher show the...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, it is my signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I used, but if any of the parties would like to verify whether the copy I just presented to the accused is the same as they have, but I take it that there are no other copies around. Then I'd like to go into the summary content of the plea agreement. The plea agreement, Mr. Cesic, includes that you have committed yourself to plead guilty on all counts of the indictment that has been brought against you. The Prosecution has committed itself to recommend to the Trial Chamber to impose a sentence within the range of 13 to 18 years. The factual basis of the plea agreement - you may remain seated, Mr. Cesic. Of course, if you want to stand, fine, but if you prefer to be seated, please do so - the factual basis of the plea agreement is contained in an attachment to the plea agreement. And I'd like to go through that in more detail. The factual basis is the following: That you, Mr. Cesic, son of Radovan, you were born on the 5th of September 1964 in Drvar Municipality in Bosnia-Herzegovina; that in May 1992, you were initially a member of the Bosnian Serb Territorial Defence in Grcica in Brcko Municipality; and that you then became a member of the Intervention Platoon assigned to the Bosnian Serb police force in Brcko town; your assigned duties during May and June 1992 included arresting specified non-Serb individuals and bringing them to the Brcko police station or the Luka detention facility for interrogation; that during the time of the alleged violations, a state of armed conflict existed in Bosnia and Herzegovina; and that you, Mr. Cesic, were aware of that fact; that during the time of the alleged violations that you were required to abide by the laws and customs governing the conduct of war, including the Geneva Conventions of 1949; and that all the acts and omissions charged against you, Mr. Cesic, as crimes against humanity, were a part of a widespread or systematic attack directed against the Muslim and Croat population of Brcko Municipality, in parts of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina designated as the Republika Srpska; and that you, Mr. Cesic, had knowledge of the wider context in which your conduct occurred. None of the victims of the charged crimes were taking active part in hostilities at the time of your conduct against them. This is the general conduct -- the general context in which the charges brought against you should be understood. Then, more specifically, the factual basis of the plea agreement includes that on about the 15th of May, 1992, that you went to the Brcko Partizan Sports Hall where Muslim civilians were being confined, and that you took the Muslim detainee Sakib Becirevic, also known as Kibe, and four other men, named Pepe, Sali, and the two sons of a man called Avdo, outside the hall, that you then, Mr. Cesic, shot and killed the five detainees with gunfire; that you intended to kill Sakib Becirevic, Pepe, Sale, and the two sons of Avdo at the time you fired your weapon at them. In respect of counts 3 and 4, because what I just read was the part related to counts 1 and 2 of the indictment, but in respect of counts 3 and 4, the factual basis of the agreement says that on or about the 9th of May, 1992, at Luka count in Brcko, you, Mr. Cesic, took a Muslim fisherman named Sejdo out from a small warehouse where he was detained, you took him out from a corner and shot him dead. You, Mr. Cesic, agree that you intended to kill Sejdo at the time you shot him. In respect of counts 5 and 6, on about the 11th of May, 1992, you called to the Muslim policeman Mirsad Glavovic from the main hangar building at Luka camp where Glavovic was being detained. You ordered Mr. Glavovic to say good-bye and shake hands with the other detainees, and then, Mr. Cesic, you took Mirsad Glavovic outside the hangar building where he and others beat -- where you and others beat and killed the victim. You also agree that you intended to kill Mirsad Glavovic at the time of the beating I just described. In respect of counts 7 and 8, the factual basis of the agreement is that on about 11th of May, 1992, at Luka camp, you, Mr. Cesic, forced at gunpoint the Muslim detainees A and B - they were brothers and they were detained in Luka camp - that you forced them to perform sexual acts, fellatio on each other, thereby causing the victims great humiliation and degradation, and at that time, Mr. Cesic, you intended that a sexual penetration of each of the victims would occur and that you knew that this was occurring without the consent of the victims. In respect of the counts 9 and 10 of the indictment against you, you agreed on the factual basis that on the 12th or the 13th of May, 1992, at Luka camp, that you and another Serb policeman used clubs to beat to death a Muslim detainee named Nihad Jasarevic, and that you intended to kill the victim at the time of the beating I just described. In respect of the counts 11 and 12 brought against you, agreed that between about the 14th of May and the 6th of June, that you took four civilians detainees whose identities are unknown to us from the office building at Luka camp to the paved road in front of the main hangar building and, with the assistance of two guards known by the names of Miso Cajevic and Pudic - of Pudic the first name is unknown - that with the assistance of two guards, you shot and killed at least two of the detainees, and that you intended to kill the victims at the time you and your associates shot them as described in the -- in what I just explained to you. This is the factual basis on which the plea agreement is concluded. Before we go into any further details of the plea agreement, I'd like to ask the parties a clarification on one issue. The indictment has charged Mr. Cesic under counts 7 and 8 - let me just find it - with committing humiliating and degrading treatment, a violation of the laws and customs of war recognised by Article 3 of the Statute of this Tribunal, and with the crime of rape, a crime against humanity under Article 5 of the Statute of this Tribunal. I'd just like to clarify whether the parties fully understand what they agreed upon in relation of this factual basis because what I just read as part of the factual basis of the plea agreement was that Mr. Cesic, that you forced two detainees to commit sexual acts in respect of the other detainee, not that you yourself did commit any of such sexual acts, nor that you personally raped one of these detainees by penetrating the bodies of these detainees. In the indictment we find that this is charged as committing these crimes, not as ordering one detainee to commit such a crime against the other, and the other against the first. I'd first like a clarification from the Prosecution on how they interpret specifically this part of the indictment, and I'd then like to seek confirmation that this is also the understanding of the Defence of this part of the indictment. Could I invite the Prosecution to clarify the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Our interpretation of this count is as follows: Both victims, both brothers are victims in this case, and both of them were used as a tool for the accused to commit the crime. He is the person who committed the crime by using the victims as a tool to commit the crime. By using one of the brothers to penetrate sexually other brother, and both of them were used as a tool. They are not perpetrators of the crime; they are not rapists, none of these brothers. It's Ranko Cesic who used them to commit rape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so I do understand that due to the situation and the threats exercised on the brothers, they couldn't make up their own mind any more, but they were in the hands of the accused who used them just as instruments to penetrate the body of the other detainee and the same the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Yes, this is our interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's your interpretation. May I ask you, Mr. Bakrac, whether this is also your understanding of committing the crimes as described in counts 7 and 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. I must admit that with my client, given the time that we've had at our disposal, that with my client, I have considered the factual aspects of the indictment against him. In factual terms, as I have discussed this with my client, this situation is not disputable. As far as I understand, we only have a disputable legal issue, and I have not discussed this with my client. What we discussed was the factual basis of counts 7 and 8. As for the factual basis of counts 7 and 8 in paragraph 14, it says that the perpetrator inflicted humiliation upon victims. We believe that the Trial Chamber would have in front of it the facts and the acts committed by the accused, regardless of the way it is formally and legally interpreted. I must say that I cannot at this point discuss the legality of this issue because I believe that in this particular case, we could agree with our learned friends from the Prosecution. But the Defence would also have a legal position of its own. I'm afraid that the position of the Defence would lead to some complications with regard to the plea agreement. Because of my own conviction that the Trial Chamber will consider the acts committed by the accused, regardless of the legal formulation of these acts, I am inclined to accept this position by the Prosecution with regard to the practical issues of the case at hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just clarify the position of the Chamber: The Chamber is aware that on the basis of the plea agreement, there is no dispute about what happened, as far as I understand. But later this morning, the accused will be asked whether he pleads guilty to a count -- or counts 7 and 8, which in the indictment appear as committing degrading and humiliation, and committing rape. So that's the legal qualification of what actually happened. I just wanted to make sure that both parties agree that these facts would amount to these crimes, specifically because in the indictment, we find only that the accused committing or, in respect of certain counts, aided and abetted, but not ordered, instigated, et cetera, et cetera. So I would like to make quite sure that the Defence understands that this behaviour where the accused, as explained in factual terms, used one of the detainees to penetrate the body of another detainee, that these facts could be qualified as committing the crime of rape in legal terms. But take your time at a later stage to discuss it with your client. I'm not asking at this moment a final answer to my question. But I just wanted to clarify this - I do agree with you - this legal issue so that there could be no misunderstanding between the parties about it. I'll then continue with the content of the plea agreement. The plea agreement further includes that you, Mr. Cesic, will not appeal any sentence between 13 and 18 years. As this Chamber has expressed in earlier cases, it might be not that clear what would happen if nevertheless Mr. Cesic would appeal, because that's up to the Appeals Chamber to decide whether any appeal in violation of that agreement could be heard or not. This Trial Chamber does not express itself on that. Mr. Cesic, you're also aware, I take it, that the agreement you reached with the Prosecution, that is, to recommend a sentence of between 13 and 18 years, does not bind this Chamber. I'd like to make sure that you fully understand that such a binding effect does not exist. Could you confirm that you understand this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cesic. Further, the agreement contains a line saying that you'll not withdraw a guilty plea once you have entered such a plea. You also understand, Mr. Cesic, I take it, that the factors the Chamber will take into consideration at sentencing will be the gravity of the events, your individual circumstances, any aggravating circumstances or any mitigating circumstances, including substantial cooperation with the Prosecutor by yourself. And you have committed yourself also to such substantial cooperation with the Office of the Prosecution. These are the main lines of what now is a public document, your plea agreement, which further contains a clause in which you give up rights you would have if you would not have pled guilty, or pleaded guilty; that is, your right to a public trial and preparing for such a trial, the right to be tried in your presence, to examine witnesses at trial, and the right not to be compelled to testify against yourself. This is a catalogue of rights you would have enjoyed if you would not have pleaded guilty. One of the rights you did not waive is to be assisted by counsel, to be represented by counsel at all stages of the proceedings. The agreement further indicates that there are no other agreements concluded between the Prosecution and the Defence, and that you entered into this agreement voluntarily. May I ask you, Mr. Bakrac, you assisted the accused in reaching this plea agreement; you also signed the agreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. According to my conscience and knowledge, I tried to discuss with the accused all the circumstances of the plea agreement. I believe that the accused has understood all this. He has accepted this plea agreement voluntarily, and that's why I put my signature on this plea agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As far as the entering into this agreement from your own free will, Mr. Cesic, you could confirm that this is how you came to this plea agreement? Voluntarily, not being forced or threatened or in whatever way?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In this case, there is no need to amend the indictment prior to hearing another plea as we heard before. At least, if the understanding of the Defence is the same as the understanding of the Prosecution in respect of counts 7 and 8, perhaps I should give you some time, Mr. Bakrac, at this very moment, before asking the accused whether he wants to change his plea, to give you an opportunity to consult with your client in respect of counts 7 and 8 so that the understanding of -- also the legal qualifications of counts 7 and 8 is fully consonant with the Office of the Prosecution. Yes, Mr. Tochilovsky.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Just a short clarification with regard to the plea agreement, under paragraph 10 of the plea agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Ranko Cesic agreed to provide full and complete interview to the OTP. And I must say that the accused has already given full and complete interview to the OTP. So this part is already addressed and fulfilled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's already completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Completed, so the cooperation has been given to the extent you expected him --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- To give the cooperation. There's no additional cooperation needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: There could be, because there's some other agreements as to testifying in other proceedings. But as to the interview, it's already fulfilled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the cooperation in respect of giving information to the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Has provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Has been completed already, and any further cooperation is -- well, in the future. But until now, the level of cooperation satisfied the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this information. Judge Liu would like to ask you a question about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think this question is addressed to the Prosecution. As you mentioned this obligation is already fulfilled, but some obligation is kind of a future obligation, that is, to testify in future proceedings before the Tribunal. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Yes. There are some further obligations, and one of them is giving testimony in future proceedings. But as you can see, there is no specific trials mentioned and no specific proceedings. So at this point, there is no determination as to the specific trial or specific case, whether the accused may testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. Well, it's very difficult to predict the future proceedings at this moment, so -- and under paragraph 15, the accused, Mr. Cesic, agrees that he will not move to withdraw this guilty plea. And on the other hand, if in the future case, the accused refuses to testify in any case, does it mean that you have the rights to withdraw from this plea agreement? Because the first sentence says clearly that "this agreement is based upon Mr. Cesic's agreement to cooperate with the Office of the Prosecutor."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Yes. In paragraph 15, it's about the guilty plea. If he pleads guilty, the understanding of both parties is that we will not withdraw this plea of guilty. As to the cooperation in future trials, I just don't have the rules before me. But under our rules, as I understand, it may affect -- the cooperation in the future with the Office of the Prosecution can affect the length of his served sentence. So he can apply to reduce the sentence or to -- at some point of serving, and the cooperation with the Prosecution is one of the main elements, one of the main criteria for such reduction. So it will affect -- it may affect in the future if the accused moved to reduce the sentence he serves. But at the time, if the question is whether we ask for postponement of sentence, sentencing procedure, until he provides this kind of cooperation, to testify in other cases, it's not our position. It should not delay sentencing, and it should not affect sentencing when sentencing time comes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, no, no, I'm not talking about sentencing procedures. I'm talking about on the one hand the accused moved to give up his right to withdraw from this plea agreement; on the other hand, on your side, you still have the right to withdraw from this plea agreement if - if - in the future, the accused refuses to testify in the future case. Is that the right understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: No, the Prosecution doesn't intend to withdraw from this plea agreement if there are any problems or questions with regard to his testimony in any other proceedings. It's not our intention, and actually now it's on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And the last one, the last question is that under paragraph 10, the last sentence, it says: "Also agree to testify in the future proceedings before the Tribunal if called upon by the OTP to do so." And on the paragraph 18, (g), "the accused waived the right to testify." Are there any contradictions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: I will just, if you allow me to explain, paragraph 18 concerns this case, because actually what is in paragraph 18, all this waiver of the rights, it's just confirmation of the consequences of the guilty plea under our rules. Because under our rules, if a person pleads guilty and the guilty plea is accepted by the Trial Chamber, the next stage is sentencing because there is no trial. As a result because there is no trial, he cannot call witnesses, he cannot put forward a Defence. Paragraph 18 just explained the consequences is under our rules -- is based on our rules and accepted by the accused. So it's only about this case, Cesic case, so it doesn't prevent him to testify in any other case. Paragraph 18 is the consequences of guilty plea under our rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your clarification. Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 76 to 80.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to turn to the Prosecution, please. In respect of the count involving rape, you have certainly very well explained that you are talking about a commission of a rape, and you understand it to mean that the accused used someone else to rape a third person, and you understand these facts as a commission of a rape committed by the accused himself. The Defence, if I understand properly, is somewhat hesitant to follow the Prosecutor when it comes to the legal qualification of the act. I should like to hear you a bit more concerning this legal issue so that the Defence can explain in more precise details their position, and so that the accused can plead in full consciousness when it comes to this particular fact, the guilty plea in respect of the crime of rape. So I should like the Prosecutor to explain to us once again briefly their position on the crime of rape as committed by the accused himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Your Honour, our position is any crime can be committed through using tools and using even physical persons, sometimes persons who are underage, who are not criminally responsible for any crimes. Using these persons as a tool. And again, I don't have the ICC Statute before me, but as far as I know, as a result of long negotiations of the parties to the ICC Statute, they drafted a practical provision in the ICC Statute exactly with this wording, that if the person used other person as a tool to commit a crime, he is the perpetrator. He committed the crime. That's what happened in this situation. Those two brothers are victims of the crime. The accused used each of them as a tool to commit sexual assault. And otherwise, we would have to come to the conclusion that both brothers are rapists and both of them are responsible for the crime which is not the case in this situation. So taken this specific situation is what the Prosecution is not the issue, it's clear that the accused used these victims as the tools to commit sexual assault. And I don't see the position of the Defence as hesitating. I understand that they need -- the Defence needs some time to consult with the client, rather than hesitation of accepting our position. But this is our position, that in this case, the accused is the perpetrator, and the victims are tools used by him to penetrate each other sexually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Bakrac, before I ask the used whether he wants to change his plea in respect of all counts, I'd like to adjourn just for a short moment so that you are in a position to consult with Mr. Cesic. And upon return, well, let's say I think 5 to 10 minutes would be sufficient, I'd like to know from you whether you need more time, or that on the basis of your consultation with your client, you could agree specifically on the issue in respect of counts 7 and 8. And if you need more time, please tell us, we'll then adjourn and continue at a later stage. If not, then we'll hear from you and we'll then continue, and I'll ask the accused whether he wants to change his plea. We'll adjourn for 5 to 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I'd like to hear from you whether your consultations with your client resulted in a position clear enough to continue or whether you would need more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I shall attempt to present the position of the Defence and the accused on this issue. And you will be able to assess what the situation is. I don't think we will need more time. I cannot a priori agree with the position of the Prosecutor as a professional lawyer. I think that if we were to simplify and look at the very specific crime, such as the rape, I think that this could have an impact on future cases, and this is the reason why when I addressed the Chamber a moment ago I said that we would provide our opinion on this issue. The crime of rape has its specificity, its special elements which distinguish it from the crime of murder. We agree that the crime of murder can be used through another person, used as a tool, as is the case with the crime of theft. When we're talking about the crime of rape, in this case we should address the issue of intent. What was the intent? Was the intent to satisfy a sexual impulse, sexual instinct or something else? It is the intent that points to the nature of the act itself and the way we are able to qualify in legal terms the act itself. On the factual side, and if we look at the factual basis which was signed by the Prosecutor, we read in points 7 and 8 that the accused forced at gunpoint Muslim detainees A and B to perform sexual acts on each other in the presence of others, thereby causing the victims A and B great humiliation and degradation. These facts show the intent. The intent was not to satisfy sexual instincts so that this could be qualified as a crime of rape, in the opinion of this Defence team. The intent goes to Article 2 of the Statute, and that is to cause great humiliation and degradation. And finally, as Defence counsel, I had to present my opinion and my position on the issue, although we didn't have a very long time, I managed to discuss the issue with my client, the accused Cesic. In view of the fact that the accused is sure that the Chamber will consider the gravity of his acts, he agrees to - when it comes to this particular count - to agree with the position of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me try to clarify the issue. I'm not quite sure that you did not mix up the intent with the motive. As far as rape is concerned, this Chamber will, in accordance with - I think it's the Kupreskic case - will understand that the intent is needed to effect the sexual penetration for whatever motive. So it's not necessary that it is intended in order to satisfy any sexual feelings of the perpetrator. But the intent should be that the actor intends this sexual penetration to take place. On the basis of the facts if, at gunpoint, you instruct someone to invade the body of another person, there might not be that much doubt as to whether that intent exists or not. In order to give you further guidance, if Mr. Cesic would plead guilty on counts 7 and 8, and especially on the count of rape as a crime against humanity, the Chamber would accept such a guilty plea on the understanding of the following: Rape can be committed not only by penetrating with part of your own body into the body of another person, but also by penetrating with any object into the body of another person. I think that's part of the -- part of the definition as given in the Kunarac case, and it would also be in accordance with the crime against humanity of rape as it has been defined in the elements of the crime, Article 7, under(1)(g) of the ICC. In both definitions, we find that's commonly accepted in many jurisdictions, that rape can also be committed by penetrating with an object in another person. The question then arises whether another person could be this object or instrument. In general terms, a person is not considered to be an object. But you could use another person as an object or an instrument if you depersonalise him, if you take from him what makes him a person; that is, his own free will. Under the circumstances as set out in the factual basis of the plea agreement, it seems that both detainees instructed to penetrate in the body of the other detainee were deprived of their own free will and, therefore, were, just as small children or insane people, deprived of what really makes them a person, a person being more than an object. Therefore, if Mr. Cesic would enter a guilty plea on count 8, when considering whether or not to accept this guilty plea, the Chamber would take this into consideration. The Chamber might even decide that if a guilty plea would be entered on count 8, to give an oral decision on whether or not to accept it, but give its reasoning in writing at a later stage in order to clarify this legal issue so that this case law which might be unprecedented - of course I'm not talking about national, but this case here - that by using the body of another person as an instrument of rape, that it should be clear on what basis such a guilty plea would be accepted. So if you would please keep in mind and if you would need more time upon this explanation to consult with Mr. Cesic, please tell us. If not, both Mr. Cesic you are aware of how the Chamber considers provisionally this legal matter, and you should keep that many mind if you take a decision on whether or not to change your plea on count 8. If you want to consult just briefly, Mr. Bakrac, there's no problem there. But put out the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, just one minute. Thank you. [Defence counsel and the accused confer].

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your indulgence, the accused will plead guilty on this count of the indictment today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Then Mr. Cesic, my next question to you is you have pleaded not guilty until now on all counts of the indictment. Do you want to change your plea?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I wish to change my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Cesic, we could read the entire indictment to you and ask you to enter a new plea on each of the counts. We also could limit ourselves to reading the counts of the indictment, counts of the indictment related to the facts we already discussed before in the context of the factual basis of the plea agreement. Would you prefer to have the entire indictment read to you, or would you be satisfied if the counts are read by the Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think it's necessary to read the entire indictment. Counts alone will suffice. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Registrar, may I ask you to read each count of the indictment, and after each count I'll ask the accused to enter his new plea.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Count 1, a violation of the laws or customs of war recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute and Article 3(1)(a) murder of the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cesic, how do you plead on count 1? Guilty or not guilty.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber records the plea of guilty on count 1. Madam Registrar, would you please read count 2.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Count 2, a crime against humanity, recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How do you plead, Mr. Cesic, guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Guilty, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber records the plea of guilty on count 2. Would you please read count 3, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Count 3, a violation of the laws or customs of war, recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute and Article 3(1)(a) of the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How do you plead, Mr. Cesic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Guilty, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber records the guilty plea on count 3. Could you please read count 4, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Count 4, a crime against humanity, recognised by Article 5(a), murder, of the Tribunal Statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How do you plead, Mr. Cesic, guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Guilty, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber records the plea of guilty on count 4. Would you please read count 5, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Count 5, a violation of the laws or customs of war, recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute, and Article 3(1)(a), murder, of the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How do you plead, Mr. Cesic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Guilty, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber records the plea of guilty on count 5. Could you please read count 6, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Count 6, a crime against humanity, recognised by Article 5(a), murder, of the Tribunal Statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you plead guilty or not guilty, Mr. Cesic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Guilty, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber records the plea of guilty on count 6 of the indictment. Madam Registrar, would you please read count 7.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Count 7, a violation of the laws or customs of war, recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute, and Article 3(1)(c), humiliating or degrading treatment, of the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cesic, do you plead guilty or not guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Guilty, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber records the plea of guilty on count 7. Would you please continue to read, Madam Registrar, count 8.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Count 8, a crime against humanity, recognised by Article 5(g), rape, which includes other form of sexual assault, of the Tribunal Statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cesic, in view of what has been discussed on the meaning of this count this morning, do you plead guilty or not guilty on count 8?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Guilty, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The chamber records the plea of guilty on count 8. Would you please read count 9, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Count 9, a violation of the laws or customs of war, recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute, and Article 3(1)(a), murder, of the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How do you plead, Mr. Cesic, on count 9?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Guilty, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber records the plea of guilty on count 9. Could you please read count 10, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Count 10, a crime against humanity recognised by Article 5(a), murder, of the Tribunal Statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cesic, how do you plead on count 10?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Guilty, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber records the plea of guilty on count 10. Could you please read count 11, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Count 11, a violation of the laws or customs of war, recognised by Article 3 of the Tribunal Statute, and Article 3(1)(a), murder, of the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cesic, how do you plead on count 11?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Guilty, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber records the plea of guilty on count 11. Could you please read count 12, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Count 12, a crime against humanity, recognised by Article 5(a), murder, of the Tribunal Statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you plead guilty or not guilty on count 12, Mr. Cesic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Guilty, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber records the plea of guilty on count 12. Mr. Cesic, the Trial Chamber now has to satisfy itself that your guilty plea on all 12 counts has been made voluntarily, that no threats or no coercion was exercised upon you, and that you were informed about the content of your plea. We already discussed it at some length in the previous stages of this hearing. The Trial Chamber has also to satisfy itself that the guilty plea is not equivocal. And finally, the Trial Chamber has to satisfy itself that the guilty plea finds a sufficient factual basis for the crime and the accused's participation therein. So your participation therein. We have dealt with you being -- the plea being informed. We have dealt with the free will on which you based your guilty pleas. I think by explaining and trying to find out what your understanding of the plea is and whether this is the same understanding as the understanding of the Prosecution of the charges brought against you, that whether the plea is or is not equivocal has been dealt with also. One of the issues that has not been dealt with now is the factual basis. The factual basis, of course, you agreed upon is what you agreed upon with the Prosecution. But this agreement as such is an important issue for an existing factual basis, but if there are any other remarkable, independent indicia, that means, any evidence that is independent from what you've told us today, I'd like to hear from the parties whether such independent indicia do exist, and whether the parties do agree on the existence of such indicia, such as testimonies of other witnesses, or whatever, documentary evidence or whatever, that would support the guilty plea entered by the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Yes, the Prosecutor has witness statements, and we have also some documentary evidence which support the charges and the facts in the factual basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Does the Defence agree that such witness statements and such material exists and supports the plea entered by the accused? Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, the Defence agrees with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. That means that the Chamber will now have to deliberate on whether it accepts the plea and whether it could decide on acceptance right away, or that we need more time. So we'll adjourn for 5 minutes. And upon return, we'll inform the parties whether a decision will be given right away or at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has decided that a decision could be delivered now. The Chamber doesn't need any more time to deliberate on whether or not to accept the guilty plea on each count. Mr. Cesic, the Chamber accepts your guilty plea on all 12 counts of the indictment brought against you as amended in November 2002. And this Chamber finds you guilty on each of the 12 counts as they have been read to you prior to entering your guilty plea. In respect of count 8, the Chamber has considered as explained before during this hearing how one detainee was used as an object or an instrument to commit rape as a crime against humanity. The Chamber will further consider whether it is appropriate to give its reasoning specifically in respect of count 8 in writing at a later stage. Please be seated, Mr. Cesic. I'd like to ask the parties about their views on how much time they need to prepare a sentencing hearing. Could I first --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We understand that you're asking for the time we need both for filing sentencing brief and for sentencing hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, those are the two stages to prepare for the sentencing hearing, how much time you would need to file the brief and how much time you would consider to be needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: For filing the sentencing brief, we would need four weeks. Say deadline, 5th November. That's how we consider. And for sentencing hearing, two more weeks, which means 19 November. And if the Chamber would allow us this time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In view of the fact that your interviews with the accused have taken already place, a slightly shorter period would be possible, let's say two or three weeks?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Yes, three weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the time needed after having studied the sentencing brief of the Defence which, we'll say, seven to ten days, would that do as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: Yes, ten days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'd then like to hear from you, Mr. Bakrac, how much time you would consider you would need in order to file a presentencing brief and prepare for the sentencing hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was going to ask the Trial Chamber to give me some time to prepare, and I agree with my learned friends, and I would kindly ask the Chamber to give me four weeks for the brief. But there is a slight difference with regard to the Prosecution. I also intend to ask the Chamber to give me an additional four weeks for the sentencing hearing. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that you would like to have some more time. On the other hand, we're now early October. If we would grant you four weeks to file your presentencing brief and another four weeks to prepare for the sentencing hearing, then we might come quite close to the winter recess. And taking into consideration that usually the Judges have their plenary meeting just briefly before the winter recess, I'd like to ask you, short of delays, would that cause you insurmountable problems? I'm putting the same question to you as I did to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with all due respect, if I have understood you correctly, the recess starts on the 19th of December. Before that, we are going to have a plenary session. What I would have in mind was the end of November, beginning of December. With all due respect, I believe that if the Defence is granted this period of time for preparation, that no series consequences would arise from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, having heard your observations in respect of the time needed, I'd like to instruct the Registrar to set a date for sentencing hearing, but not until you have consulted with the Chamber after this hearing. Is there anything else, any other motion or any other submission to be made by the parties at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOCHILOVSKY
utterances.text: No, no submission by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing from the Defence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll adjourn, and the Chamber will give a scheduling order in respect of the filing of presentencing briefs. And after having consulted with the Registrar, you'll hear from the Registry when a sentencing hearing is scheduled. We stay adjourned.
